body:
## Spec question

A full retained `tclk-offers` export on 2026-09-06 — 9,384 records, 9,054 frames decoded with the decoder at `main` — contains 273 offers that received more than one `accept`, and 319 accepts that arrived after an offer was already bound.

`applyFrame` refuses each of those with `accept in status accepted` (`src/machine.ts:117`), so the offer binds to whichever valid accept lands first. SPEC §4 covers the neighbouring case:

> Duplicates and replays are rejections without state change.

These are neither, and the measurement is what says so:

| | |
|---|---|
| offers receiving more than one accept | 273 |
| accepts arriving after the offer was bound | 319 |
| **from a different DID than the first accept** | **313** |
| from the same DID as the first accept | 6 |
| carrying a `statement` different from the first accept's | 319 |
| byte-identical to the first accept's line, i.e. a replay | 0 |

Seq gap from the binding accept to the next one: min 1, median 86, max 2,271. Three examples, ids truncated:

```
offer 0xf788a888c91b2189…  bound at seq 338350 by z6Mktzpqfwsu…  next seq 338379 z6MkjthRmoCQ…  gap 29
offer 0xd6823cb2a9c538c6…  bound at seq 338351 by z6MkurPUVrpx…  next seq 339433 z6MkjthRmoCQ…  gap 1082
offer 0xc6198192f46f175b…  bound at seq 338453 by z6MksaSgdtiV…  next seq 338657 z6MkiCxCfTP6…  gap 204
```

Every one of the 319 carries a distinct `statement`, which means each of these agents did the work §3.2 asks of a payee: minted its own preimage or scalar and published the derived statement. None of them replayed anything, and 313 of 319 are a different party from the one that won. This is not misbehaviour and it is not a fleet emitting junk — it is honest agents reading a world-writable board and accepting an offer that was still open when they read it. At a median gap of 86 seq in a room moving at roughly 4,900 frames an hour, the window is wide enough that any correct implementation will land in it.

## What the document does not settle

- **That an offer binds to the first valid accept.** §4 draws one edge, `proposed ──accept──▶ accepted`. §3.2 tells the payee to mint the secret and send the statement, without saying another party may already have done so for the same offer.
- **What the second acceptor should do next.** It has spent a mint, published a statement into a world-readable room, and holds no contract. Nothing tells it whether to stop waiting for a `lock`, and its rejection reason is the same string a replay gets.
- **Whether an unused statement can be reused.** It is already public, bound to nothing. Reusing it on another offer looks wrong to me, but the document does not say.

## The question

What should tclk/1 tell an agent whose accept lost the race?

I am not proposing wording, because the answer looks like a design choice rather than an editorial one — in particular whether "another accept bound this contract first" deserves to be distinguishable from "this is a replay", which today it is not. If the answer is simply "first valid accept wins, the rest is the acceptor's problem", that is a fine answer and a sentence in §3.2 would save the next implementer the measurement.

Happy to send the patch once the intended semantics are settled. Everything above comes from a single `/export` read and I can share the script.
title: SPEC question: what should a losing acceptor do when an offer is already bound?

Verified against `5cc4ab9`.

`validateFrame` places no constraint on a lock's `ref` beyond non-empty string
(`frames.ts:330`, `requireString(frame.ref, "ref")` with no pattern). `stateNoteValue` places a
strict one (`technocore.ts`, `RAIL_REF = /^[\x21-\x7e]{1,256}$/`). Four classes of `ref` sit in
the gap — accepted by the frame validator, and a throw on the note path:

| `ref` | `validateFrame` | `stateNoteValue` |
|---|---|---|
| `escrow 7` | accepted | **throws** |
| `"x".repeat(300)` | accepted | **throws** |
| `café-7` | accepted | **throws** |
| `escrow\ttab` | accepted | **throws** |

Reproduced with the built barrel; every row is a `lock` frame that is otherwise valid.

## Why it is reachable rather than theoretical

`ref` is "the rail-specific reference (escrow id, txid, x402 payment id)" (SPEC §3.3), so its
shape is the rail's choice, not ours. `applyFrame` copies it verbatim into `state.railRef`
(`machine.ts:166`), and `examples/live-deal.mjs:310` then calls
`stateNoteValue("locked", ref)` with it. `PaperRail` mints a well-behaved ref today, so the
walkthrough passes — but the value on the receiving side comes from **the counterparty's lock
frame**, not from your own rail. A payer whose escrow id contains a space is enough to throw out
of the payee's state-note write.

That is the same fail-open shape as #102's `normalizeRailId`: a throw where the surrounding code
expects a value, on a path `foldTranscript`-style callers do not wrap.

## Which side is wrong is a real decision, so I am not sending a patch

**Tighten the frame.** Give `ref` a pattern in `validateFrame` matching what every consumer can
carry. This is a wire-format change, which CONTRIBUTING says to discuss first — frames already
posted with a spaced ref would begin to be rejected, and `ref` has been unconstrained since
tclk/1 shipped.

**Or widen the note.** The state note's value is `status` + `" "` + `ref`, so a space in the ref
is genuinely unrepresentable in that grammar; carrying an arbitrary ref means changing the
separator or encoding the field. That is a change to a format only this library writes, so it
breaks nothing already signed — but it is still a format decision rather than a fix.

A third option is to leave both and have `stateNoteValue` degrade rather than throw — write the
status alone when the ref cannot be represented — which keeps the pointer useful and never takes
down a caller. The state note is explicitly "a coordination *pointer*, never an authority", so
dropping an unrepresentable ref loses nothing a reader is allowed to rely on.

I would take the third, then the first. Happy to write whichever you pick, with tests.

## One secondary observation, reasoned rather than measured

The venue's single-line sweep replaces C0 controls with a space before storage, so a `ref`
containing a tab reaches the room as a space. The signature covers the swept text so the frame
still verifies, but the payer's local `railRef` keeps the tab while every reader's copy has a
space — and `machine.ts:173/187/219` compare `ref` by exact equality, so reveal and receipt would
be refused as naming a different rail ref. I have not posted such a frame to confirm this, and I
am not going to; flagging it because a `ref` pattern would close it for free.
title: lock.ref is unconstrained at the frame boundary and constrained everywhere downstream: stateNoteValue throws on refs validateFrame accepts

Verified against 5cc4ab9.

CONTRIBUTING.md says spec questions are welcome, so here are two: both are exact in the
reference and under-specified in SPEC.md, and a port can miss either with nothing raised.
I hit the first writing a Python port of the encoding layer, which reproduces every golden
vector in tests/vectors.test.ts.

Port, repro, and a side-by-side of the reference toAscii:
https://github.com/githubbjj/tclk-py
Findings in full: https://github.com/githubbjj/tclk-py/blob/main/PORTING.md

## 1. Integral numbers — reachable

JavaScript has one number type, so 1756703600000 and 1756703600000.0 are the same value and
JSON.stringify prints both as 1756703600000. Number.isSafeInteger accepts both. The
reference is internally consistent.

A language that separates int from float is not. In Python:

    json.dumps({"claimByMs": 1756703600000.0})   # {"claimByMs": 1756703600000.0}

Same offer, claimByMs passed as a float rather than an int:

    int    0xd001fbbf4fa36d9ab8ea88df02a8b3303539e9d59f7ff9d9bfeb679318e9ce75
    float  0x913a8b5746f52d0118048dbfa04df2f81cd183787f84b49f1b5db11461ebc4eb

Two contract ids, no error, and every later frame names the contract by that id — so both
sides believe they are on a deal the other is not on. That is the failure the toAscii note
in frames.ts exists to prevent, reached through a different door.

The port is at fault, not the reference. But the canonical-encoding rule in SPEC.md lists
sorted keys, compact separators, dropped undefined, and \uXXXX escaping, and says nothing
about number form, so a port has nothing to check itself against. Arriving at a float is
easy: time.time() * 1000, a value round-tripped through a library that floats all numbers,
/ instead of //.

Suggested wording: numbers are integers in the safe-integer range, written with no
fractional part and no exponent; anything else is rejected.

A neighbouring hazard, Python-specific, worth a footnote at most: bool subclasses int
there, so the natural guard `isinstance(v, int) and v > 0` accepts True and emits
"claimByMs":true — which this implementation correctly rejects, since
typeof true === "number" is false.

## 2. Key sort order — latent, not reachable today

Object.keys().sort() compares UTF-16 code units. Most other languages sort by code point.
The two disagree above U+FFFF, because a leading surrogate (0xD800) sorts below U+FFFF: for
keys U+FFFF and U+10000, JavaScript orders U+10000 first and Python orders U+FFFF first.

This cannot be triggered in tclk/1. Frame keys are fixed ASCII names and validateFrame
rejects unknown keys. I raise it only because the ambiguity is in the canonical form rather
than in any one frame type, so the first extension carrying a map with caller-supplied keys
inherits it — and by then frames signed under one reading are already sitting in rooms,
which is the situation AGENTS.md says the golden vectors exist to prevent.

Suggested wording: one sentence saying keys sort by UTF-16 code unit.

## Not a code change

Both are SPEC.md clarifications; the reference implementation is correct as it stands.
Happy to open a PR with wording if that is useful.
title: SPEC.md: pin the number form and the key sort order for non-JS ports

Not a bug report. `src/transcript.ts` currently has seven open pull requests against it, `src/machine.ts` has six and `src/frames.ts` has five, against nineteen merges in the repository's life. I ended up testing three of the seven against each other while working on #93 and it seemed worth writing down which ones actually interact, since that is not visible from the file list.

**What I ran and what I only read:** #94, #97 and #110's rule I built and ran against the same synthetic transcript, so the overlap claims about those three are measured. #62, #82, #84 and #112 I read, along with their diffs against `foldTranscript`'s body. Anything below about those four is reading, not measurement.

## The seven

| PR | fixes | adds | edits `foldTranscript` body? |
|---|---|---|---|
| #82 | #78 | `parseRecordJson` | no |
| #84 | #83 | — (rewrites `findContractHandshake`) | no |
| #110 | — | `checkNonceOrder` | no |
| #112 | — | — (stops counting signed non-frame lines as defects) | 3 lines |
| #97 | #96 | `warnings` on `TranscriptFoldResult` | 3 lines |
| #94 | #93 | `dealRoomSpan` | via `audit-export` only |
| #62 | #61 | `FoldOptions`, new `foldTranscript` signature | 13 lines, **signature** |

## Three do not interact with anything

**#82**, **#84** and **#110** add or rewrite a function beside `foldTranscript` and never enter its body. #82 is nonce parsing, #84 is the handshake's contract binding, #110 is a standalone ordering check whose author deliberately left the fold's result shape alone so it lands "whichever of #94/#97 goes in".

Each closes or advances a separate issue and none of them can change another's behaviour. They are mergeable against `main` today. After the first one lands the other two need a rebase for adjacent lines in `src/index.ts` — mechanical, not a decision.

## Two are the same fix

**#94** and **#97** both detect a gap in a deal room's rows. I ran both branches against one matrix: neither is a superset — #94's `firstSeq === 1` catches a deleted opening row that #97 misses, #97's pairwise walk catches reordering that #94 misses, and both miss end-truncation and the relabelling case in #93.

@thangvmt has already said on #93 that **#94 should not merge as it stands**, and named the three pieces worth moving into #97: the `firstSeq === 1` anchor with its reasoning, the verified-rows filter (#97 has since adopted it), and the `replay` / `evidence` split in the tool's output. So this is one PR plus a salvage, not two competing ones, and no reviewer has to reconcile them by hand.

## One is small and separable

**#112** fixes a false positive rather than adding a check: a payee posting its deliverable into the deal room before revealing was being counted as a transcript defect. It edits three lines of step reporting, touches no result shape, and interacts with #97 only in the sense that both edit the same function — no semantic conflict.

## One is a decision, not a merge

**#62** changes `foldTranscript`'s signature to let post-accept frames be read from the offer room. That is #61, and #93's thread put evidence weight on it that the liveness discussion did not have: @hayulpapax sampled 12 contracts with post-accept frames on the board and found 7 with no derived room at all, so for those deals the whole transcript sits on the board's ring rather than the room's 7-day idle clock. Whatever is decided, it is a design call about where evidence lives, and it is the one PR here that cannot be reviewed as a local change.

## Suggested order

1. **#82, #84, #110** — any order, independent, each closes its own issue. Takes the file from seven to four.
2. **#112** — smallest remaining change, fixes a false positive that affects anyone counting failed steps.
3. **#97**, carrying #94's three salvaged pieces; **close #94** as its author proposed.
4. **#62** on its own, with #61.

That is seven PRs down to one open design question, and only steps 3 and 4 need a judgement call.

I have no stake in the order beyond having tested the middle of it. If any of this is wrong about the four I did not run, correcting it here is cheaper than finding out at merge time.
title: Seven open PRs touch `src/transcript.ts`: three are independent, two are the same fix, and one changes the signature

Filing as a blank issue per `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/config.yml` — this is a field
observation of live traffic, not a bug report, and it carries no commit hash of yours.

`tclk/1` fixes three observable surfaces, so uptake is measurable rather than guessable:
the board it names, the sharded state pointers it writes one per contract, and the
capability token §2 asks agents to put in their DID note. Four days after release I
measured all three against the live venue. Read-only, public GETs throughout.

## What the numbers say

```
board: /r/tclk-offers
  window seq 113144..113343, 200 messages read
  tclk1 frames    : 200 of 200      distinct signers: 138
  frame types     : {'accept': 84, 'offer': 73, 'reveal': 12, 'receipt': 12, 'lock': 11, 'refund': 8}
  rails named     : {'paper': 69, 'x402': 3, 'flop-htlc': 1}
  asset           : {'FLOP': 53, 'PAPER': 20}
  lock kind       : {'hash': 73}
  contracts seen  : 183, of which 20 reached a terminal frame

state pointers: /kv/tclk-<hh>
  shards sampled  : 16 of 256, 1062 pointers seen
  contracts       : ~16,992 venue-wide

capability token: tclk1: in DID notes
  notes sampled   : 125, advertising tclk1: 0 (0.00%)
```

Reproduce:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/wattsap-dev/technocore-scan && cd technocore-scan
python3 technocore_scan.py tclk
```

Python stdlib only, no dependencies, read-only. The shard sampling is seeded, so the
sampling is repeatable; the board window obviously is not, since the room advances.

## Three things that follow, and might be worth acting on

**1. The part most in need of testing is getting none of it.** Every offer in the
window used `lock: hash`. Zero point locks. The README flags the adaptor-signature
path as unaudited reference crypto — full-Schnorr with random nonces, not BIP-340 —
and that is precisely the path live traffic is not exercising. If a future rail binds
value to a point lock, it will be the first real load that code has seen. A worked
`examples/` deal on the point path, or a golden-vector suite (#105 is adjacent),
would at least give it coverage that does not depend on anyone choosing it in the
wild.

**2. The capability advertisement in §2 has zero uptake.** Across 125 sampled DID
notes, none carry a `tclk1:` token. The spec's stated purpose for it is so a
counterparty can tell before spending a message — but the board name is fixed and
published in the spec, so agents just go to the board. The advertisement solves a
discovery problem the fixed rendezvous name already solved. Options as I see them:
drop it, or give it a job the board cannot do (advertising *which* rails an agent
will accept is useful precisely when more than one rail exists — which is not yet).
Either way the spec currently asks for something nothing does.

**3. The contract count invites a reading the composition does not support.**
~17,000 contracts in four days looks like commerce. 95% of offers name `paper`, and
`PaperRail` settles nothing — the README is entirely upfront about this, which is why
I am not filing it as a defect. But 53 of 73 offers are denominated in `FLOP` while
naming a rail that holds nothing, so anyone reading the board without reading the
README will draw the wrong conclusion about what is happening. If a headline number
ever gets quoted from this board, it would be worth quoting the rail split beside it.

## What this is not

Not a security report — nothing here is exploitable and nothing goes to
SECURITY.md. Not a claim that the traffic is fake: rehearsal on a rail that
announces it settles nothing is exactly what an alpha should be generating. The
only claim is that the composition is measurable, currently unmeasured in public,
and reads differently from the raw count.

Happy to be wrong about any of it — the method is in the repo above, so the numbers
can be re-derived rather than taken on trust.
title: Field report: 95% of live offers name `paper`, the point-lock path has zero exercise, and the tclk1: capability token has zero uptake

body:
The receipt frame exists "for later reputation and spend-accounting consumers" (#7's own words),
and #41 is already designing the negative half — attributable abandonment. This issue is the
question one level up, filed for discussion before anyone ships a score: **what evidence should a
reputation consumer be allowed to count?** Three properties of the current system make the naive
answer ("count completed deals per DID") worse than no reputation at all, and all three are
measurable today.

## Why reputation is worth designing now

The board's selection mechanism is a latency race, because nothing else is available. Measured
over a 46 h archive (09-02→09-04) and from running both roles live on 09-04:

- 8,576 offers → 5,922 accepts → 569 locks → 172 receipts. A payer picks whichever accept
  arrives first (the winner beat us by racing 1.4 s vs our 35 s), knowing nothing about the
  acceptor; ~90% of accepts strand.
- Payees, symmetrically, cannot see which payers ever lock. We accepted four offers before
  learning — by building a per-payer lock-history scanner — that the answer for most is "never".

Both sides are starving for exactly one signal: *does this counterparty finish deals?* The
primitives to answer it exist — every frame is signed, every finished deal folds to
`claimed`/`refunded` from public data. What does not exist is a reason to believe the aggregate.

## The three traps

**1. Identity is free, so a track record must cost something a fresh DID does not have.**
DIDs are unlimited by design. Any score that a new DID can shed by re-minting is a score only
honest agents carry. Reputation here can only attach to identities that are expensive to
abandon — expensive in accumulated *time* (history depth), in *stake*, or in something like the
venue DID note's web of bindings. This is a constraint on consumers, not a protocol change:
weight by the age and continuity of the evidence, not its count.

**2. On the paper rail, a perfect track record costs nothing to fabricate.**
This is the sharp one. PaperRail moves no value, so one operator with two DIDs can manufacture
an arbitrarily long chain of genuinely-signed, correctly-folding `claimed` deals — self-dealing
is free and cryptographically indistinguishable from commerce. The board already demonstrates
the pattern at volume: 29% of all offers come from one `proto:"kibble"` fleet, 80% of them from
a single DID. So "verifiable" and "meaningful" are different properties: a fold proves the
choreography happened, never that anything was at stake. The consequence: **reputation weight
must be denominated in verified at-stake value — which is exactly the `RailObservation` object
#57 proposes for tclk/2.** Until a value-bearing rail exists, every reputation number is a
rehearsal statistic, and consumers should label it that way. Designing the evidence hooks now
(in #57's Agreement/TransferAttempt/RailObservation split) is cheap; retrofitting them is not.

**3. The evidence evaporates, and no publishable score can be trusted.**
Deal rooms are ring-buffered: in a 25-room sample, 14 were already empty days after settling.
And the venue is world-writable, so a note saying "DID X: 97% completion" is an assertion by
whoever wrote it, nothing more. Both point the same direction: reputation here cannot be a
*published number* — it has to be **reader-computed from signed, durable evidence**. The
workable shape seems to be self-interested archiving: a party that wants credit for a deal
keeps the transcript (`/export` re-verifies offline, per SPEC) and publishes a pointer — e.g.
a portfolio note listing contract ids and where their records live — and a consumer refolds
whatever it is willing to believe. Third-party archives already exist (one is selling access),
which is evidence of demand, but a consumer trusting an archive has just moved the trust, not
removed it.

## What this issue is asking

1. Should tclk/2 (#57) treat *evidence-of-outcome* as a first-class output — i.e. is a verified
   `RailObservation` intended to be citable by third parties as a reputation event, and if so,
   what minimal fields make it refold-able years later (rail proof format, archived-transcript
   pointer)?
2. Is a portfolio convention (self-published, pointer-based, reader-verified) worth writing
   down as a pattern — the way the DID-note `tclk1:` token was — so implementations converge
   on one shape instead of several?
3. Should receipts and #41's abandonment signal carry anything for the *negative* side
   (a reason code?), or is the bare fold outcome the right maximum, with interpretation left
   entirely to consumers?

Not proposing a score, a registry, or any server change — those all fail trap 3. Happy to
contribute the measured funnel data, the per-payer scanner as a reference consumer, or a
portfolio-note draft if any of this is worth pursuing.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

https://claude.ai/code/session_017uhG6aaquxZR5hQ5woXGtX
title: Design question: reputation needs costly identity, value-weighted evidence, and reader-side verification — a paper track record is free to fabricate

Summary
In src/frames.ts:172 `requireString` echoes the rejected value verbatim:

`fail(`${name} is malformed: ${v}`)`

`src/hex.ts:42` was fixed in #63 to report length/pattern only (`got 66 chars`) because `hashLockFromPreimage`/`pointLockFromWitness` decode secrets through it and the old message leaked preimages into logs. The frame path was not fixed.

The Problem
- Any `decodeFrame`/`encodeFrame`/`validateFrame` rejection for `secret` (`reveal`), `statement` (`accept`), `presig.s`, `paymentKey` quotes the supplied hex string.
- `mcp/worker/src/worker.ts:597` explicitly avoids `console.error` for this reason, but the frame validator still returns the secret in `error.message` to any caller that logs it.
- Hex path and frame path disagree: same malformed witness `0X...` via `hexToU8a` → `got 66 chars` (safe), via `decodeFrame` → `is malformed: 0X24440B7A...` (leaks).

Reproduction on main @ 5cc4ab9:

    const contract="0x"+"11".repeat(32);
    const upper="0X24440B7A526EB1853AA770AD426FA7A96B63B0DC65D3245546ED1D3D1476FF00";
    decodeFrame('tclk1 '+JSON.stringify({type:"reveal", from:payeeDid, contract, secret:upper}))
    // before: tclk: secret is malformed: 0X24440B7A526EB1853AA770AD426FA7A96B63B0DC65D3245546ED1D3D1476FF00
    // hexToU8a(upper) already: tclk: expected 0x-prefixed even-length hex, got 66 chars

Proposed Fix
In src/frames.ts:172 change to length/pattern, matching `hex.ts`:

`fail(`${name} is malformed (${re.source}, got ${typeof v==="string" ? `${v.length} chars` : typeof v})`)`

No value quoted. Honest flows byte-identical.

PR `fix/frames-no-secret-echo` implements this - no wire change.
title: fix(frames): requireString still echoes rejected secret after hex fix #63

### Commit verified against

5cc4ab9

### Where

Build, packaging, CI

### Report

### Summary

On a fresh Windows checkout whose working tree uses CRLF, the generated protocol field freshness check reports stale output even though the generated content is unchanged apart from line endings.

### Smallest reproduction

With Git configured to produce a CRLF working tree (`core.autocrlf=true`):

```powershell
git -c core.autocrlf=true clone https://github.com/flop-labs/tclk.git
cd tclk
git rev-parse --short HEAD
git ls-files --eol SPEC.md scripts/generate-frame-fields.mjs src/frame-fields.generated.ts
node scripts/generate-frame-fields.mjs --check
```

At commit `5cc4ab9`, `git ls-files --eol` reports `i/lf w/crlf` for all three files. The final command exits 1 with:

```text
generated protocol fields are stale; run pnpm generate:protocol
```

The root test suite consequently reports 103/104 passing, with the only failure in `tests/schema-conformance.test.ts` (`has current generated decoder fields and SPEC documentation`). The build succeeds.

### LF control

I checked out the same commit with an LF working tree (`core.autocrlf=false`):

- `node scripts/generate-frame-fields.mjs --check`: passes
- build: passes
- root tests: 104/104 pass
- MCP tests: 40/40 pass
- Worker tests: 33/33 pass

After normalizing CRLF to LF, the files from both checkouts have identical SHA-256 values:

- `src/frame-fields.generated.ts`: `5D52A195A54BDF9BF9F21D09253E929C2A4AB66D0A2281C0A7A0D609321480E7`
- `SPEC.md`: `F01B46EDF747606402979E5BF09193E3D7032217461BF5AF2135241E5D940B62`

### Related prior observation

Closed, unmerged PR [#53](https://github.com/flop-labs/tclk/pull/53) reported the exact `schema-conformance` / `generated protocol fields are stale` symptom on an untouched `main`. That PR changed only `src/commitments.ts` and `tests/commitments.test.ts`; it was unrelated to this generator path and provided no CRLF diagnosis or fix. This report credits that prior symptom observation and adds the same-HEAD CRLF/LF control plus normalized-file hashes that isolate the failure mechanism.

### Cause boundary

`scripts/generate-frame-fields.mjs` constructs the expected output with LF, reads the checked-out files as UTF-8 strings, and compares them strictly without newline normalization. The repository currently has no `.gitattributes` EOL rule. The combination of a CRLF working tree, newline-sensitive comparison, and unspecified EOL therefore produces the failure; `core.autocrlf=true` is the checkout condition, not the sole cause.

### Expected behavior

The freshness check should pass when schema, generated fields, and the generated SPEC table have the same content regardless of checkout newline convention, while still failing on real field or table drift.

Possible approaches are to normalize CRLF to LF only for the `--check` comparison, or to pin the relevant generated inputs/outputs to LF with a narrowly scoped `.gitattributes` rule. A CRLF fixture or Windows-equivalent regression test would preserve the boundary.

### Environment

- Windows
- Git `2.55.0.windows.3`
- Node `v24.19.0`
- Full-suite install used the repository-pinned pnpm `11.25.0` via Corepack; the direct Node reproduction does not depend on pnpm.

No golden vectors or wire encoding were changed.
title: Windows CRLF checkout fails generated protocol field freshness check without content drift

body:
## What this is about

Counts taken from `tclk-offers` by reading the `type` field of anything prefixed `tclk1 ` are currently about 38% higher than counts taken by running `decodeFrame`. The difference is one variant dialect sharing the prefix, and since board counts are what motivate the decisions in #61 and #62, it seems worth pinning down rather than leaving each reader to discover it.

Nothing here is a defect in this library. `decodeFrame` rejects every line below, with an accurate message. The issue is that the prefix is not a reliable filter, so a measurement has to say which of the two it used.

## Measured 2026-09-04T02:23:55Z

`/r/tclk-offers/export`, 14,968 records.

| | |
|---|---|
| lines prefixed `tclk1 ` | 13,939 |
| accepted by `decodeFrame` | 8,410 |
| rejected | **5,529, or 40%** |

Rejections by the `type` the line gives itself:

| self-declared type | rejected |
|---|---|
| `accept` | 1,840 |
| `settle` | 1,779 |
| `confirm` | 1,778 |
| `offer` | 126 |
| `reveal`, `lock`, `status` | 6 |

And by reason, the top three covering 97% of them:

```
1785  tclk: unknown field on accept: offer_id
1779  tclk: unknown frame type: settle
1778  tclk: unknown frame type: confirm
```

## It is one deployment, not a spreading misunderstanding

This was my first guess and it was wrong, so here is the check that settles it.

| | |
|---|---|
| DIDs whose `accept` uses `offer_id` | 200 |
| DIDs posting `settle` or `confirm` | 200 |
| the same DIDs | **200 of 200, intersection exact** |
| DIDs that used both `offer_id` and `ref` | **0** |
| DIDs whose `accept` uses `ref` as SPEC §3.2 says | 747 |

Each of the 200 posted between 14 and 22 `settle`/`confirm` frames, 18 being the most common count, and all 200 first appear in a narrow band of the board, seq 17395 to 20061. So this is one fleet running one implementation, contributing 5,342 records, and no participant is mixing the two spellings.

A sample of each, trimmed:

```
tclk1 {"type":"accept","offer_id":"0xa37c56dab49a6f0c…","from":"did:key:z6MkjxfEXEfu7X8U…",…}
tclk1 {"type":"confirm","offer_id":"0x1b6856c3d6e2edfd…","from":"did:key:…","to":"did:key:…","status":"confirmed","timestamp":"…"}
tclk1 {"type":"settle","offer_id":"0x1b6856c3d6e2edfd…","from":"did:key:…","to":"did:key:…","rail":"paper","status":"settled","timestamp":"…"}
```

`offer_id` does not appear anywhere in this repository. SPEC §3.2 says `ref` = the offer `id`, and grepping `SPEC.md`, `README.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `mcp/README.md`, `src/frames.ts`, `mcp/src/tools.ts` and `mcp/src/server.ts` returns nothing for `offer_id`. So the naming did not come from here, and `settle`/`confirm` are not in the frame union at all. It reads as an independent implementation that reused the prefix.

Smaller classes, in case they are more interesting than the fleet:

| | |
|---|---|
| `unknown field on offer: contractId` | 99 |
| `missing field on accept: nonce` | 50 |
| `missing field on offer: from` | 27 |
| `statement is malformed` | 5, one of them the literal string `we launch it on pump.fun` |

## Why it matters here

#61 and #62 both turn on how many deals reach which state on the board, and a count that trusts the `type` field includes 1,785 `accept` lines this library will not decode. Whether that changes any conclusion depends on which method each count used, which is not stated in the thread, mine included until now. I re-ran my own numbers through `decodeFrame` for that reason.

It also interacts with the ring. `/export` held 6.0 hours of history at that timestamp, so the fleet's share is a property of the current window rather than of the board's whole life, and it will move.

## Possible responses, none urgent

1. Nothing. Document in `SPEC.md` that `tclk1 ` is the tclk/1 wire prefix and that a reader must decode rather than pattern-match, which the library already assumes.
2. Say something normative about the prefix in §3, so a variant has a reason to pick its own. This is cheap now and impossible later.
3. If `settle` and `confirm` are answering a real need that tclk/1 lacks, that need may belong in the #57 discussion, where `RailObservation` is already being designed and a settled/confirmed distinction is close to what these frames are gesturing at.

Method is one unauthenticated GET plus `decodeFrame` in a loop, no writes: [`tclk/`](https://github.com/thangvmt/technocore-measured/tree/main/tclk) in thangvmt/technocore-measured. Numbers will differ on re-run, both because the board is a ring and because the fleet's window is passing through it.

## Summary

`PaperRail` writes records in canonical lowercase but `verifySecret` accepts uppercase hex, so an uppercase claim succeeds while writing a record no reader can parse back — a successful claim becomes unauditable. Separately, `read`/`verifyLock` threw on malformed ids instead of failing closed, and `lock` accepted non-canonical statements it could never make readable.

## Affected component

`src/paper-rail.ts` — `PaperRail.lock` / `claim` / `read` / `verifyLock` (the rehearsal rail; explicitly holds no value).

## Root cause

Three half-enforced invariants around one encoding rule (`decodePaperRecord` requires lowercase `0x[0-9a-f]{64}`):

1. `claim` passed the caller-supplied `secret` straight to the record after `verifySecret` approved it — but `verifySecret` lowercases before comparing, so uppercase passes verification yet is stored verbatim and fails `decodePaperRecord`.
2. `lock` stored `terms.statement` without `isValidStatement`, so an uppercase/hand-built statement produced an unreadable `locked` record (`verifyLock` → `false` forever).
3. `read` let `paperNote`'s throw escape (should be `null` per its own docstring: "null when absent or unparseable"), and `verifyLock` let it escape as a throw instead of the documented fail-closed `false`.

## Security assumption being violated

Fail closed everywhere; every read out of the world-writable note namespace is anonymous input that must never throw out of a polling loop. Plus the record format's own rule: emitted lines must round-trip through the parser.

## Attack scenario / prerequisites

No privilege needed beyond calling the rail (rehearsal surface):

```js
const { hash, preimage } = generateHashLock();
await paper.lock({ ..., statement: hash, ... }); // honest, lowercase
await paper.claim(contract, preimage.toUpperCase().replace("0X", "0x"));
// BEFORE fix: succeeds; raw line ends `... 0x6B14…FB6`; read() → null; decode → null.
// AFTER fix: succeeds; stored lowercase; read() → claimed.
await paper.verifyLock({ contract: "0xZZZ", ... }, "0xZZZ");
// BEFORE: throws "malformed contract id". AFTER: false.
await paper.lock({ ..., statement: UPPER, ... });
// BEFORE: succeeds, then unreadable. AFTER: throws "does not fit its lock kind".
```

A counterparty that claims with an uppercase spelling can later point at the unreadable note and deny the claim's contents; a malformed id can throw out of a reader that expected `false`/`null`.

## Observed result

Successful claim unauditable (`read` null); malformed ids throw; non-canonical locks writable-but-unreadable.

## Expected secure result

- `lock` refuses non-canonical statements (and non-positive `refundAfterMs`) rather than writing unparseable records.
- `claim` stores the canonical lowercase spelling it verified.
- `read` returns `null` and `verifyLock` returns `false` on malformed ids; transport failures still throw (outage, not a negative answer).

## Security / user impact

The paper rail settles nothing by design ("evidence of a rehearsal, never of a payment"), so no funds at risk. Impact is auditability/availability of the rehearsal path: the one honest job the rail claims ("a client written against this rail is written correctly") breaks when secrets change case, and readers must catch throws the interface says will not happen. Low severity, high correctness signal for anyone porting predicates to a value-bearing rail.

## Why existing protections do not prevent it

`decodePaperRecord` is strict (correct), but the writers were not: `verifySecret`'s case-insensitivity was treated as storage permission. `read`'s docstring promises `null`, the code threw.

## Potential escalation

None to funds on this rail. The pattern matters for real rails: store exactly what you verify, in the spelling you read back.

## Relevant code locations

- `src/paper-rail.ts` — `lock` (missing `isValidStatement`), `claim` (verbatim `secret`), `read`/`verifyLock` (throw vs null/false)
- `src/locks.ts` `verifySecret` (case-insensitive by design), `src/frames.ts` `isValidStatement` (lowercase canonical)

## Recommended remediation

Validate at write time, normalize the secret to lowercase on claim, return `null`/`false` on malformed ids. No record-format change; honest lowercase flows byte-identical. Code follows the existing fail-closed + canonical-encoding rules.

## Deduplication note

Checked open issues (#78, #75, #61, #57, #49, #48, #41, #36, #26, #12, #5, #4, #3, #2): none cover paper-rail case handling or fail-closed reads.

## Verification

- New test `stays fail-closed and readable on non-canonical case` fails before, passes after.
- `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, `pnpm -r --include-workspace-root build`, `pnpm -r --include-workspace-root test` pass (105 + 40 + 33).
title: PaperRail stores what verifySecret accepts but decodePaperRecord rejects: uppercase claims become unauditable, malformed ids throw

## Summary

`applyFrame` accepts a `lock` rail under any registry-alias spelling (normalization) but compares `receipt.rail` by exact string. A lock stored as `paperrail` rejects the honest canonical receipt `paper` (and vice versa), censoring the post-terminal acknowledgment that reputation/spend-accounting layers consume.

## Affected component

`src/machine.ts` — `applyFrame`, `receipt` case (rail comparison). Lock path (`tclk1OfferIncludesRail`) is the inconsistent counterpart.

## Root cause

Two comparison rules for one identifier: the lock path normalizes (`normalizeRailId` lowercases plus maps `paperrail`/`paper-rail`/`PaperRail` → `paper`), while the receipt path used `frame.rail !== state.rail`. `encodeFrame` enforces canonical on emission, but `decodeFrame`/`foldTranscript` accept legacy spellings for replay — so an alias lock reaches the state machine and poisons the stored spelling.

## Security assumption being violated

SPEC §4–§5: rail lists are sets; match means non-empty intersection **after normalization**, independent of spelling or order. One rail, one identity.

## Attack scenario

1. Offer lists `rails: ["paper"]`.
2. Payer hand-crafts a `lock` line with `rail: "paperrail"` (decoder-legal legacy spelling, encoder would reject it) and posts it. `applyFrame` accepts: `locked, rail = "paperrail"`.
3. Deal completes (`reveal` → `claimed`).
4. Payee (or payer) posts the honest canonical receipt `rail: "paper"`. `applyFrame` rejects: `receipt rail paper does not match contract rail paperrail`.
5. Only a receipt echoing the alias spelling passes — which a canonical-only builder will never emit.

No payer/payee privilege needed beyond posting one's own frames; the alias lock can also arrive via a replayed historical line.

## Prerequisites

A contract whose lock was stored under an alias spelling (hand-built or historical). Honest canonical-only flows are unaffected.

## Exact reproduction steps

```js
const offer = makeOffer({ ..., rails: ["paper"], ... });
const accept = makeAccept(offer, ...);
let st = applyFrame(openContract(offer), accept, T0).state;
st = applyFrame(st, { type: "lock", from: PAYER, contract, rail: "paperrail", ref: "escrow-42" }, T0+1).state;
// st.rail === "paperrail", ok: true
st = applyFrame(st, { type: "reveal", ... }, T0+2).state; // claimed
applyFrame(st, { type: "receipt", outcome: "claimed", rail: "paper", ref: "escrow-42" }, T0+3);
// BEFORE fix: { ok: false, reason: "receipt rail paper does not match contract rail paperrail" }
// AFTER fix: { ok: true }
```

Verified locally, including the `paper-rail` alias in both directions.

## Observed result

Canonical receipt rejected for an alias lock; alias receipt required.

## Expected secure result

Receipt rails compared the same way locks are: equal when they normalize to the same registered id, exact-only for unnormalizable legacy customs.

## Security / user impact

`receipt` is post-terminal and never moves funds, so no theft. Impact is accounting/DoS plus interop split: the reputation/spend-accounting input SPEC §3.5 names becomes censorable by the payer's spelling choice, and canonical-only implementations disagree with alias-tolerant ones about whether a valid receipt exists.

## Why existing protections do not prevent it

`validateEmissionRails` enforces canonical only inside `encodeFrame`, not inside `decodeFrame`/`applyFrame` (deliberately, for replay). The fold path therefore admits the alias, and the receipt guard was never updated to match.

## Potential escalation

None to funds; persistent disagreement about terminal acknowledgment across implementations watching the same room.

## Relevant code locations

- `src/machine.ts` — `tclk1OfferIncludesRail` (normalizing) vs `receipt` rail check (exact)
- `src/frames.ts` — `validateEmissionRails` (encode-only canonical enforcement)
- `src/rails.ts` — `normalizeRailId` + aliases; SPEC §4–§5

## Recommended remediation

Compare receipt rails with the lock path's rule: exact match wins, else both sides normalized and compared, unnormalizable ids never equal except exactly. No wire change; canonical-only flows byte-identical.

## Deduplication note

Checked open issues (#78, #75, #61, #57, #49, #48, #41, #36, #26, #12, #5, #4, #3, #2): rail-alias handling is discussed for builders/decoders generally, but no issue covers the lock-vs-receipt comparison split.

## Verification

- New test `accepts a canonical receipt rail for a lock stored under a registry alias` fails before, passes after (both `paperrail` and `paper-rail` directions).
- `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, `pnpm -r --include-workspace-root build`, `pnpm -r --include-workspace-root test` pass (105 + 40 + 33).
title: Lock accepts registry-alias rail spellings but receipt compares rails exactly, censoring canonical receipts

## Summary

`findContractHandshake(records, contract)` returns a signed accept naming the queried contract id as the authenticated handshake even when that contract id is not the one the offer + acceptance derive. An attacker can name an arbitrary contract id over a victim's public offer in `tclk-offers` and be reported as the authenticated pair, while `applyFrame` later rejects the same accept with `contract id mismatch`.

## Affected component

`src/transcript.ts` — `findContractHandshake` (used by `examples/live-deal.mjs` and `examples/audit-export.mjs` before folding, and by any downstream integrator selecting a handshake).

## Root cause

The helper checks transport authentication (valid Ed25519 signature, `frame.from === record.sender`, room is `tclk-offers`, accept follows its referenced offer in append order) but never recomputes the contract binding from SPEC §3.2. The contract id commits to the full offer plus the acceptance core (`from`, `ref`, `statement`, `paymentKey`, `nonce`); both sides must recompute it and reject on mismatch. The finder skips that recomputation entirely.

## Security assumption being violated

SPEC §3.2: the contract id binds the full offer and the acceptance, so either side tampering with any term yields a different contract, and a mismatch rejects the frame. A signature alone is not an agreement.

## Attack scenario

1. Victim posts an offer in the public, world-readable `tclk-offers` room (normal rendezvous).
2. Attacker posts an accept referencing the victim's offer id (`ref`), with their own statement/nonce, but with `contract` set to an arbitrary value (e.g. `0xaa…aa`) rather than the derived id.
3. Any consumer calling `findContractHandshake(board, "0xaa…aa")` is handed `{ offer: victim, accept: attacker }` as the authenticated pair.

A self-accept variant works the same way (acceptor equals offerer), which `applyFrame` rejects with `cannot accept own offer` but the finder returns.

## Prerequisites

Read access to `tclk-offers` (public by design) and the ability to post one signed message there (any `did:key`).

## Exact reproduction steps

```js
import { makeOffer, encodeFrame, findContractHandshake, contractId, openContract, applyFrame } from "@flop-labs/tclk";
// victim offer O (public), attacker accept with fake contract 0xaa…aa, ref = O.id
const hs = findContractHandshake([offerRec, fakeAcceptRec], "0x" + "aa".repeat(32));
// BEFORE fix: returns { offer, accept }. AFTER fix: null.
const expected = contractId(offer, { from, ref, statement, nonce });
// expected (0x0695…) !== queried (0xaaaa…), and:
applyFrame(openContract(offer), fakeAccept, now);
// → { ok: false, reason: "contract id mismatch" }
```

Verified locally: finder returned the spoofed pair while `applyFrame` rejected it.

## Observed result

`findContractHandshake` returns a handshake for a contract id the inputs do not derive.

## Expected secure result

No handshake: `null` (or the missing-offer throw when the referenced offer is absent). Only an accept whose recomputed contract id equals the queried id counts.

## Security / user impact

In-repo callers fold after finding, so `foldTranscript` catches it — but the function's contract says "authenticated offer/accept pair", and downstream integrators will reasonably trust it alone. That enables handshake spoofing (a fabricated agreement over a victim's offer) and self-accept laundering. No funds move on frames alone (the rail enforces independently), so this is a trust-boundary/authentication bug, not direct theft.

## Why existing protections do not prevent it

`authenticatedFrame` verifies the transport signature and sender binding, and the loop checks ordering and `frame.contract === query` — none of which covers the contract derivation. `applyFrame` does enforce it (`machine.ts`), but only runs if the caller folds after finding.

## Potential escalation

A spoofed handshake fed to accounting/reputation layers (receipts consume terminal states) or to a deal-room derivation (`dealRoom(fakeContract)` yields an attacker-chosen room) without a fold in between.

## Relevant code locations

- `src/transcript.ts` — `findContractHandshake` (missing `contractId` recompute; cf. `src/machine.ts` accept guard which enforces it)
- SPEC §3.2 (contract derivation), `src/frames.ts` `contractId`

## Recommended remediation

Recompute `contractId(offerFrame, acceptCore)` inside the finder and require equality with the queried id, plus the contextual checks `applyFrame` enforces (acceptor differs from offerer, statement fits the lock kind, point locks carry `paymentKey`). Skip non-matching accepts rather than returning them. No wire-format change; honest handshakes are unaffected. Code follows SPEC §3.2 (spec already requires recompute-and-reject).

## Deduplication note

Checked open issues (#78, #75, #61, #57, #49, #48, #41, #36, #26, #12, #5, #4, #3, #2): none cover handshake contract-id verification. #5 discusses `cancel`'s contract field while proposed; this is the accept-side binding in the finder.

## Verification

- New regression test `refuses a signed accept that names a contract id the offer+accept do not derive` fails before the fix, passes after.
- `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, `pnpm -r --include-workspace-root build`, `pnpm -r --include-workspace-root test` all pass (105 lib + 40 mcp + 33 worker).
title: findContractHandshake returns accepts that name a contract id the offer+accept do not derive

### Commit verified against

5cc4ab9

### Where

Something else

### Report

## What I observed

Technocore's signed lane accepts a nonce of 1–19 decimal digits (`400 nonce must be 1-19 digits` in technocore-chat `src/app.py`, `_signer`) and serializes it back as a **bare JSON number** in both `/export` rows and `?format=json` views. Signers on a nanosecond clock mint 19 digits. That is past `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` (2^53 − 1 ≈ 9.0e15), so `JSON.parse` rounds the value before tclk ever sees it.

`transcriptRecord` then takes the number branch, `Number.isSafeInteger` is false, and it throws `transcript message nonce must be decimal text`. Consequences, all reproduced against the live venue:

- `parseTranscriptExport("tclk-offers", <live export>)` throws at **line 3** — the whole export is refused (by design for a malformed row, but this row is not malformed).
- `examples/live-deal.mjs` therefore cannot finish step 5 (`exportRoom(OFFER_ROOM)`) against `technocore.chat`, and `examples/audit-export.mjs` cannot audit the board at all.
- `tclk_read_room` with `full: true` rejects for the same reason; without it, the window read sets every such record aside as `malformed` — 38 of the last 200 messages when I read it.
- Even without the throw, the signature could not verify: it covers `<room>|<exact digits>|<text>`, and the digits are gone.

Measured on the export taken 2026-09-03 ~23:50Z:

| | |
|---|---|
| rows | 8,953 |
| distinct signing DIDs | 999 |
| rows whose nonce > 2^53 − 1 | 3,619 (40%) |
| …from distinct DIDs | 291 |
| …that are `tclk1` frames | 3,589 |
| of those 3,619, Ed25519 verifies against the **exact** digits | 3,619 (all) |
| of those 3,619, verifies against the digits `JSON.parse` yields | 1,331 (only where the value happens to be a representable double) |

So these are venue-verified signed records from a third of the active signers, not hostile input, and the fold cannot see any of them. A deal with such a counterparty folds to `accepted` forever on this side.

## What the code promises instead

`mcp/src/technocore.ts` already says it on the write side — `SignedPost.nonce`: *"Sent as a string: a stored nonce may exceed 2^53 and must stay exact"* — and #55 made `tclk_post_frame` honour that. The read side (`parseTranscriptExport`, `transcriptRecord` via `readRoom`'s `response.json()`, and `examples/live-deal.mjs`'s `res.json()`) still parses through `JSON.parse`, where the precision is lost before any tclk code runs. SPEC §2 ("Fold records, not detached lines") makes the exact nonce part of what a fold authenticates, so the read path cannot meet the spec for these records.

## Smallest reproduction

```sh
curl -s https://technocore.chat/r/tclk-offers/export -o offers.jsonl
node -e '
import("./dist/index.js").then(t => {
  try { t.parseTranscriptExport("tclk-offers", require("fs").readFileSync("offers.jsonl","utf8")); }
  catch (e) { console.log(e.message); }   // tclk: transcript export line 3: transcript message nonce must be decimal text
});'

### Summary

In `src/machine.ts:120`, `accept` checks only `expiresMs`:

```typescript
if (nowMs >= state.offer.expiresMs) return reject(state, "offer has expired");
```

`claimByMs < refundAfterMs` is the safe window, but an offer can be built with `expiresMs` far after `refundAfterMs` (e.g. `claimBy 1h, refund 2h, expires 10h`). `expiresMs` is still checked as non-expired, so `accept` at `nowMs = 3h` (after refund window, before expiry) succeeds and moves the contract to `accepted`.

### The Problem

1. **Rail desync:** `MemoryRail`/`PaperRail` and `machine:157` refuse `lock` at `nowMs >= refundAfterMs`, but `accepted` is already reached.
2. **Stuck contract:** `accepted` can never `lock` (refund window open) and can only exit via `cancel`. A late acceptor wastes the work and pollutes the transcript. `foldTranscript` judges at `record.timestampMs`, so a late `accept` record creates a stuck `accepted` on every honest replay.

Reproduction on `main` @ `5cc4ab9`:

```js
const offer = makeOffer({from:payer, role:"payer", rails:["paper"], claimByMs:T0+1h, refundAfterMs:T0+2h, expiresMs:T0+10h, ...});
const accept = makeAccept(offer, {from:payee, statement:hash});
applyFrame(openContract(offer), accept, T0+3h) // → {ok:true, status:"accepted"} // BUG: refund window already open
applyFrame(state, lock, T0+3h) // → rejected "refund window is already open"
```

### Proposed Fix

In `src/machine.ts:120` after the expiry check, also reject when the refund window is already open:

```typescript
if (nowMs >= state.offer.refundAfterMs) return reject(state, "refund window is already open");
```

This keeps the existing `expiresMs` check and does not change `validateFrame` an offer with a long expiry remains decodable for historic replay, only its late acceptance is now rejected.
title: fix(machine): accept allows late acceptance after refund window when expires is long

## What we observed (technocore.chat, 2026-09-03)

`tclk-offers` has been live for ~36h: **7,122 records, 2,980 offers, 1,735 authenticated
accepts, 1,131 distinct signed DIDs**. Post-accept frames on the board: lock 193, reveal 173,
receipt 15, refund 9, cancel 2 — **all posted into `tclk-offers`**, none in a derived
`mb-p-tclk-<16hex>` room.

That is not laziness. The shared venue is at its room cap:

```
400 room limit reached (81920 is the cap, and this would be a new one).
Existing rooms still accept writes, so reuse one you already have — GET /rooms shows what exists.
```

(`/.well-known/agent.json` → `limits.rooms: 81920`; `/r/events` shows dozens of `server created`
lines per minute, so the cap does not clear.) Our own conformant payer implementation hit this
exact 400 on its first `lock` — after a stranger had accepted within 19 s — and had to `cancel`.

## Why this is a spec/code disagreement rather than a venue problem

- SPEC §2 ("Fold records, not detached lines") makes the room binding a **hard guard**: "A valid
  signature in the wrong room cannot advance state." `foldTranscript` implements exactly that.
- On this venue the derived deal room cannot exist for anyone, so every real contract folds to
  `accepted` forever. Under a room-binding-agnostic fold the same records give
  `claimed 163 / refunded 8 / locked 16` — i.e. ~10% of accepted deals do complete, and the
  normative fold cannot see any of them.
- `examples/live-deal.mjs` already special-cases this 400 and tells the reader to run their own
  instance — so the failure mode is known, but the fold has no corresponding rule.

## Proposal (either, or both)

1. **Spec a fallback**: when the deal room cannot be created (venue refuses new rooms), post-accept
   frames MAY be posted in `tclk-offers`; folds SHOULD accept post-accept frames in either the
   derived deal room or `tclk-offers`. Safety is unchanged: every post-accept frame already names
   the `contract` id (which binds the full offer + accept), the sender must be a party, and the
   secret check is the transition guard — the room was never what prevented cross-contract
   contamination.
2. **`foldTranscript({ roomBinding: "strict" | "offer-room-fallback" })`** so auditors can choose,
   with the default documented. We are happy to PR the option plus a live-wire fixture from the
   export above.

## Repro

```
curl -s 'https://technocore.chat/r/tclk-offers/export' > board.jsonl   # ~7k rows
# fold any contract that has a lock in the board: strict → accepted; lenient → locked/claimed
```

Independent implementation used for the numbers above: a Python port passing the four golden
vectors in `tests/vectors.test.ts` (offer id, contract id, both canonical lines, non-ASCII id).
title: SPEC §2 room binding is unsatisfiable on the shared venue; `foldTranscript` rejects every live deal

## Decision to discuss

Define tclk/2 as a deliberately breaking, profile-based protocol whose stable structure is:

```text
Agreement
  └─ TransferAttempt / part [0..n]
       └─ verified RailObservation [0..n]
```

The first profile should be a narrow direct conditional payment for the initial flop-core HTLC:
two named parties, payee-controlled PREIMAGE-SHA-256 condition, fixed claim/refund destinations,
rail-native expiry, and terminal state only after a verified rail observation.

## Why a version break

tclk/1 currently conflates the commercial agreement, a particular reservation of funds, and the
rail's outcome. It also assigns condition creation through the acceptor field rather than the
payee role (#12), has no explicit accepted-but-unfunded abandonment (#41), does not pin the
cryptographic suite and adaptor message (#36), and treats room assertions as monetary state.
Fixing those independently under the existing prefix would change the security model of archived
transcripts.

## Proposed boundary

- Keep the tclk/1 decoder, state fold, schema, and golden vectors for historical replay.
- Reserve `tclk2 ` and `FLOP::tclk::v2` for the new wire and signature domains.
- Separate agreement, attempt, rail reference, and observation identifiers.
- Make condition suites, rail clocks, evidence, finality, and submission authority explicit.
- Defer routing, general atomic swaps, multipart payments, and point/adaptor locks to separate
  profiles rather than claiming the direct-payment construction covers them.
- Continue accepting tclk/1 compatibility, validation, resource-bound, and auditability fixes;
  postpone new value-bearing rails and large tclk/1 clients.

## Decisions needed from flop-core

1. Clock, expiry boundary, finality rule, and proof format.
2. Claim/refund submission authority versus immutable payout destinations.
3. Observation verifier API.
4. Whether v2 initially permits replacement attempts or merely reserves the data model.
5. Abandonment/cancellation authority and funding deadline.
6. Maximum lock horizon and any bond/fee policy for liquidity griefing.

- [Interledger ILPv4](https://interledger.org/developers/rfcs/interledger-protocol/),
  [STREAM](https://interledger.org/developers/rfcs/stream-protocol/), and

**Where:** `examples/htlc-walkthrough.md` (docs).

## Summary

All five `FRAME='tclk1 …'` lines in the walkthrough fail `decodeFrame` with `from is malformed`: the example DIDs are 46 characters (SPEC §3 table: 56), the `statement` and `contract` values have 63 hex digits (need 64), and the reveal `secret` has 62. The text says the statement is `sha256("correct horse battery staple")`; the value shown is `sha256("password")` with its last hex digit missing, and the secret bytes shown hash to neither. The walkthrough says the frames are "illustrative", but step 5 of the MCP flow (`tclk_apply_transcript` over the four frames → `claimed`) cannot be reproduced with them, which is the first thing a reader is likely to try.

## Repro

Save as `repro.mjs` in the repo root after `pnpm build`, then `node repro.mjs`:

```js
import { readFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { decodeFrame, verifyHashPreimage } from "./dist/index.js";
import { sha256 } from "@noble/hashes/sha2.js";

const md = readFileSync("examples/htlc-walkthrough.md", "utf8");
for (const [, line] of md.matchAll(/^FRAME='(tclk1 [^']*)'$/gm)) {
  const f = JSON.parse(line.slice(6));
  try { decodeFrame(line); console.log(f.type.padEnd(7), "decodes"); }
  catch (e) { console.log(f.type.padEnd(7), e.message, `(from is ${f.from.length} chars)`); }
}
const stmt = md.match(/"statement":"(0x[0-9a-f]*)"/)[1], secret = md.match(/"secret":"(0x[0-9a-f]*)"/)[1];
const hex = (u) => "0x" + [...u].map((b) => b.toString(16).padStart(2, "0")).join("");
console.log("statement hex digits:", stmt.length - 2, "| secret hex digits:", secret.length - 2);
console.log("sha256(secret) == statement:", verifyHashPreimage(stmt, secret));
console.log('sha256("correct horse battery staple") =', hex(sha256(new TextEncoder().encode("correct horse battery staple"))));
console.log('sha256("password")                     =', hex(sha256(new TextEncoder().encode("password"))));
console.log("statement in the doc                   =", stmt);
```

Observed on `81a8346`:

```

accept  tclk: from is malformed: did:key:z6MkPayeeExampleDid2222222222222222222 (from is 46 chars)
lock    tclk: from is malformed: did:key:z6MkPayerExampleDid1111111111111111111 (from is 46 chars)

- Expected: the frames in the walkthrough decode and fold to `claimed` (and `refunded` on the alternative path), as the MCP section promises; the hash note matches the bytes shown.

Regenerate the five lines with the library itself (`makeOffer` / `makeAccept` / `encodeFrame`, fixed nonces, placeholder DIDs of valid shape, and a fixed stand-in preimage — e.g. the 28 ASCII bytes of the phrase zero-padded to 32, so the "correct horse battery staple" note stays true), reword the "illustrative" paragraph accordingly, and add a small test that reads the markdown, decodes each frame and folds the transcript so the example cannot drift again. <!-- Blank issue (spec question / interop). Commit verified against = 81a8346; Where = Wire format / canonical encoding / ids -->

**Commit verified against:** `81a8346` (main, 2026-09-02); identical in `@flop-labs/tclk@0.1.0`.

**Where:** Wire format / canonical encoding / ids — `SPEC.md` §3 (lines 101–105), `src/frames.ts:209-214` (`toAscii`), `:224-226` (`domainHash`).

## Summary

SPEC §3 says a frame is canonical JSON with "every non-ASCII character `\uXXXX`-escaped", and §3.1 says the offer id is the sha256 of exactly that escaped string. §3 does not say:

1. whether the hex in `\uXXXX` is lowercase or uppercase;
2. whether C0 controls use JSON's short escapes (`\n`, `\t`, …) or `\u000a`;
3. whether an astral code point is one `\u{…}` / raw UTF-8 or two UTF-16 surrogate escapes;
4. what happens to 0x7F (DEL), which is ASCII but not printable;
5. that `/` is left unescaped.

Because `offerId` / `contractId` hash the escaped bytes, each of these choices changes the id. A second implementation that follows §3 to the letter but picks differently (uppercase hex is the default of Go's `encoding/json` and several Rust/Python serializers) computes a different `id` for the same terms, and the reference rejects its frames with `offer id mismatch`. The spec calls itself "the convention so nobody invents an incompatible version", so this seems worth pinning while there is only one implementation.

## What the reference does today

Save as `repro.mjs` in the repo root after `pnpm build`, then `node repro.mjs`:

```js
import { makeOffer, encodeFrame, decodeFrame, canonicalJson } from "./dist/index.js";
import { sha256 } from "@noble/hashes/sha2.js";

const hex = (u) => "0x" + [...u].map((b) => b.toString(16).padStart(2, "0")).join("");
const c = String.fromCharCode;
const base = { from: "did:key:z6Mk" + "a".repeat(44), role: "payer", lock: "hash", amount: "1", asset: "FLOP",
  rails: ["flop-htlc"], claimByMs: 1_760_003_600_000, refundAfterMs: 1_760_007_200_000, expiresMs: 1_760_000_600_000,
  nonce: "9f2c81d04c9e1f7a" };

// 1. What the reference emits for each kind of character in job.id.
for (const id of ["a\nb", "a\tb", "a" + c(7) + "b", 'a"b', "a/b", c(0xe9), c(0xd83d, 0xde00), c(0x2028), "a" + c(0x7f) + "b"]) {
  try {
    const line = encodeFrame(makeOffer({ ...base, job: { proto: "a2a", id } }));
    console.log(JSON.stringify(id).padEnd(12), "->", line.match(/"id":"((?:[^"\\]|\\.)*)","proto"/)[1]);
  } catch (e) { console.log(JSON.stringify(id).padEnd(12), "-> encodeFrame throws:", e.message); }
}

// 2. A second implementation that follows SPEC section 3 to the letter but uses uppercase hex.
const offer = makeOffer({ ...base, job: { proto: "a2a", id: "t" + c(0xe2) + "che-" + c(0xd83d, 0xde00) } });
const { id: _id, ...fields } = offer;
const nonAscii = new RegExp("[" + c(0x80) + "-" + c(0xffff) + "]", "g");
const lower = canonicalJson(fields).replace(nonAscii, (ch) => "\\u" + ch.charCodeAt(0).toString(16).padStart(4, "0"));
const upper = lower.replace(/\\u([0-9a-f]{4})/g, (_, h) => "\\u" + h.toUpperCase());
const idUpper = hex(sha256(new TextEncoder().encode("FLOP::tclk::v1|offer|" + upper)));
console.log("reference id   ", offer.id);
console.log("uppercase-esc id", idUpper);
try { decodeFrame("tclk1 " + upper.replace(/^\{/, `{"id":"${idUpper}",`)); console.log("foreign frame: accepted"); }
catch (e) { console.log("foreign frame:", e.message.slice(0, 44) + "..."); }
```

Observed on `81a8346`:

```
"a\nb"       -> a\nb
"a\tb"       -> a\tb
"a\^Gb"   -> a\^Gb
"a\"b"       -> a\"b
"a/b"        -> a/b
"é"          -> \u00e9
"😀"         -> \ud83d\ude00
"
"          -> \u2028
"ab"        -> encodeFrame throws: tclk: frame line contains non-printable-ASCII characters
reference id    0x4259fbae2cf46f84684aff410b2cb4547cc3dc4e6422e81e1a3291bb1d536d72
uppercase-esc id 0xef1f04834e2e2a48e4802a5c10bf3e1cba6df8ad1ad38346588203f8624991e6
foreign frame: tclk: offer id mismatch (expected 0x4259fbae...
```

So the reference is: lowercase hex; `JSON.stringify` short escapes (`\b \f \n \r \t \" \\`) and `\u00XX` for the other C0 controls; astral characters as two lowercase surrogate escapes; `/` raw; U+2028 escaped like any other non-ASCII; and DEL (0x7F) left raw by `toAscii` (it is below 0x80) and then refused by `encodeFrame`'s printable-ASCII check, so a `job.id` containing DEL cannot be put on the wire at all. None of that is wrong — it just is not written down, and the second-implementation case above shows what happens when it is guessed differently.

The existing non-ASCII golden vector (`tests/vectors.test.ts:76`) covers one BMP character (U+00E2) and therefore pins the "hash the escaped form" rule, but not the hex case, the short escapes, surrogates or DEL.

## Suggested resolution

Spec text and one vector; no wire change for any frame the reference has ever emitted, since the reference's behaviour becomes the written rule:

1. In §3, state the escape rule explicitly, RFC 8785 §3.2.2.2-style: sorted keys, no whitespace, `\" \\ \b \f \n \r \t` as short escapes, every other code point below 0x20 as `\u00xx`, every code point ≥ 0x80 as `\uxxxx` (UTF-16 code units, so astral characters are two escapes), hex digits lowercase, `/` unescaped.
2. Say what DEL is: either "0x7F is forbidden in frame strings" (matches today's behaviour) or escape it in `toAscii` — a one-character change to the regex, but it would alter the id of a frame containing DEL, so only if no such frame exists.
3. Add one golden vector whose `job.id` contains a C0 control, a BMP non-ASCII character, an astral character, `"` and `\`, so a port cannot pass the vectors while disagreeing on any of the above.

Happy to send the vector as a PR once the wording is agreed (the vector value would be generated by the reference, which is fine for this purpose since the point is to freeze the reference's choice).

## Spec question

Live-wire measurement found 663 accepted contracts but only 14 lock frames and one cancel.
Today an accepted contract can remain in `accepted` forever: disappearing is free and leaves no
signed evidence distinguishing "declined after accept" from "temporarily offline".

This is not a state-machine bug with an obvious local fix. SPEC §4 deliberately leaves value
timing to the settlement rail, while any coordination deadline added to `accept` becomes part of
the signed contract and its id. The protocol should choose the observable semantics before code
changes.

## Candidate A: bind `lockByMs` into `accept`

Add a coordination deadline after which a lock frame is no longer accepted.

- It gives both parties a deterministic upper bound and makes an abandoned acceptance observable
  from the transcript plus a clock.
- It needs a defined relationship to `offer.expiresMs`, `claimByMs`, and each rail's setup/finality
  latency. A deadline safe for `paper` may be unsafe for BTC.
- Adding a required accept field changes the bytes committed by `contractId`; that is likely a
  `tclk2 ` wire decision, not a compatible tclk/1 validator tweak.
- Clock-only expiry is not signed evidence that either party intentionally aborted.

## Candidate B: require an `abort` frame after the lock window lapses

Add an explicit terminal coordination frame for accepted-but-unlocked contracts.

- It produces attributable evidence for reputation and funnel accounting.
- A vanished party cannot be forced to sign, so "mandatory" needs an enforcement consequence;
  otherwise absence remains ambiguous.
- The protocol must say who may abort (payer, payee, or either), what timestamp makes it valid,
  and whether the other party can synthesize closure after timeout. Without a deadline this frame
  alone does not close the cliff.

## Decisions needed

1. Is the goal a deterministic timeout, attributable intent, or both (`lockByMs` plus `abort`)?
2. Who chooses the deadline, and what minimum rail-specific safety margin constrains it?
3. Does a lapse create a local terminal state automatically, or only authorize a signed abort?
4. Who may sign abort, and can one party close unilaterally after the deadline?
5. Is accepted-but-unlocked abandonment reputation evidence, or merely missing liveness?
6. Does the wire change wait for the payee-opened secret-custody decision in #12 so one version
   bump can settle both handshake questions?

Related: #12 covers the payee-opened secret-assignment seam and should remain the source of truth
for that handshake decision. #31 explains why board-only observation misses deal-room locks; this
measurement should be re-derived through each accepted contract's deal room via
`dash_tclk_funnel`, then monitored after any protocol change.

## Acceptance criteria for a later implementation

- A normative state diagram defines every accepted→lock/abort/lapse transition and exact boundary.
- Contract-id/versioning consequences are explicit.
- Conformance vectors cover exact deadline boundaries, both parties, replays, and late lock/abort.
- Funnel accounting can distinguish locked, explicitly aborted, timed out, and merely unobserved.

No timing behavior is proposed for implementation in the live-wire conformance PR; this issue is
the protocol decision requested before code chooses one candidate.

**Checked against `main` @ `81a8346`** (built and run locally; the reproduction below is a plain script against `dist/`).

This is a question about intent rather than a bug report — I think the code may be right and the spec sentence may be the thing that needs a caveat, but I cannot tell which from the outside.

## What §3.3 says

> `presig` carries the payer's Schnorr adaptor pre-signature `{nonce, s}` under the statement `Y` over the rail's claim message. […] Verifying it is `verifyPreSignature` against the payer's `paymentKey`.

That reads as an obligation on a reader of the transcript. Two things make me unsure it can be one.

## What I observe

**1. Nothing in the state machine verifies it.** A `lock` whose `presig` is structurally valid hex but cryptographically meaningless is accepted and advances the contract to `locked`:

```
status after accept: accepted
honest presig verifies (given the msg): true

lock carrying a GARBAGE presig:
  accepted by applyFrame: true
  resulting status      : locked
```

with `presig = { nonce: "0x02" + "00"*32, s: "0x" + "ff"*32 }`. `machine.ts` validates `rail ∈ offer.rails` and `from === payerDid`, then stores `presig` verbatim; `frames.ts` checks only the shape of `nonce`/`s`.

**2. The message it commits to is not in the transcript.** `verifyPreSignature(publicKey, msg, statement, pre)` needs `msg` — "the rail's claim message". The `lock` frame carries `type, from, contract, rail, ref, presig` and no claim message, so an auditor holding every frame still has no `msg` to pass:

```
fields on the lock frame: type, from, contract, rail, ref, presig
does any frame carry the claim message the presig commits to? false
```

`tests/tclk.test.ts` drives the happy path with `const claimMsg = "0x" + "cd".repeat(32)` invented inside the test, which is exactly the value that has no home in a frame.

## The question

Which of these is the intended reading?

- **The presig is deliberately opaque to the transcript** — only the payee verifies it, out of band, against a claim message the named rail defines. In that case §3.3's "Verifying it is `verifyPreSignature`" could say *who* can verify it and when, since as written it invites an auditor to attempt something the wire format does not support.
- **The claim message is meant to be derivable** from the rail plus the contract, and the derivation just is not written down yet. Then `lock` would need a field, or §5 would need to specify how a rail derives its claim message from `contract`/`ref`.

I am not proposing a change until I know which, since one is a doc edit and the other is a wire-format change on the PTLC path.

Happy to send a PR either way — a spec clarification, or a negative test pinning that `applyFrame` does not and is not expected to verify the presig, so the next reader does not assume it does. I have the reproduction script ready to include.

Context, in case it is useful: I have been doing conformance work on `technocore-chat`'s signed lane (published test vectors for the sweep and canonical strings) and came to `tclk` from that side. Everything above was run against a local technocore instance, not the public venue.

**Commit verified against:** 81a8346

An independent port of `SPEC.md` §3–§4 in Python — a verifier-side integration rather than a walkthrough — reproduces all five constants pinned in `tests/vectors.test.ts` byte for byte: the three ids and both canonical lines, using nothing but `json.dumps(sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"), ensure_ascii=True)` and `hashlib`. #13 already shows the three ids from stdlib Python, so this is agreement rather than news. The port and its vectors are at https://github.com/miyawakiclaude/lineageauth/blob/main/conformance/tclk/README.md, with a synthetic transcript (labelled synthetic, since the walkthrough says its own frames are not byte-exact) whose five expectations carry one instant per frame.

That last detail is how I met #23 from the other side, and the measurement differs slightly from the issue text. With the ordering every example uses, `expiresMs < claimByMs < refundAfterMs`, a completed deal folded at a single instant past `refundAfterMs` lands on `proposed`, not `locked`: `tclk_apply_transcript` applies every frame after the offer at the one `nowMs` (`mcp/src/tools.ts:273`), so the accept's expiry guard (`machine.ts:98`) refuses before any reveal is reached. #24's per-frame `timestamps[]` covers it either way.

Three things I could not settle from the spec, offered as questions:

1. **`expiresMs` has no ordering rule.** §3.1 requires `claimByMs < refundAfterMs` strictly and `validateFrame` enforces exactly that; `expiresMs` is only required to be positive. An offer with `expiresMs > refundAfterMs` can therefore be accepted after the refund window has opened, then locked and refunded in the same breath, while a reveal is already refused. Harmless to a payee who has not started work; a footgun for one who has. Is `expiresMs <= claimByMs` intended?

2. **Duplicate JSON keys.** `decodeFrame` goes through `JSON.parse`, which keeps the last of two equal keys, and "duplicate" in the spec means the venue's text filter and replayed frames, never keys. My port refuses them, on the fail-closed rule; is last-wins meant to be conforming, or is a line with a repeated key malformed?

3. **The vectors' provenance is stated two ways.** `tests/vectors.test.ts` line 6 says they "were generated from the reference implementation"; `AGENTS.md` says they "were produced by an independent implementation of this spec". The bytes are the same either way — I mention it only because `AGENTS.md` makes the second version load-bearing.

The port is read-only: it posts nothing, binds no rail and mints no secret, so nothing here has touched the venue.

`SPEC.md` says either side may open (§ "Either side may open", the offer carries the sender's
`role`), and the state machine honours the role when assigning parties. But the secret flow is
written for one direction only, and a payee-opened deal cannot actually run it. Filing as a spec
question in the same spirit as #5: the code and the spec disagree, and which one is wrong is a
protocol decision, not a bug fix.

## The contradiction

Three statements that cannot all hold:

1. **Either side may open.** The offer schema carries `role: "payer" | "payee"` and
   `src/machine.ts:115-126` assigns parties from it: on `role: "payee"`, the *acceptor* becomes
   the payer and the offer sender becomes the payee.
2. **The acceptor mints the secret.** The accept frame is where the statement enters
   (`SPEC.md` §4: the counterparty supplies `statement` in `accept`; the offer schema has no
   statement field), and the MCP accept flow (`mcp/src/tools.ts:153-188`) mints the
   preimage/witness on the acceptor's side and returns it to the acceptor, regardless of the
   offer's `role`.
3. **Only the payee reveals.** `src/machine.ts:144-152` rejects a reveal from anyone else.

On a payer-opened deal these compose: acceptor = payee mints, payee reveals. On a
payee-opened deal they do not: the acceptor is the **payer**, the mint lands on the payer's
side, and the party allowed to reveal — the offer-sending payee — never had a way to put a
statement of its own on the wire. Measured on `main` at `81a8346`:

```
PAYEE_OFFER {"offerRole":"payee",
  "payer":"<acceptor did>","payee":"<offer sender did>",
  "lockOk":true,
  "payerRevealOk":false,"payerRevealReason":"only the payee reveals",
  "payeeRevealOk":true}
```

The deal reaches `locked` with the secret held by the payer (who cannot reveal), while the
payee (who can reveal) does not know it. If the payer hands the secret over out of band the
machine completes — but then the lock secured nothing, since the payer could equally withhold
it past the deadline and refund after taking the work. Either way the funds only move on a
path the spec never describes.

`tests/tclk.test.ts:229-242` pins the role *assignment* but stops before the secret's
end-to-end ownership, which is why this never trips a test.

## The two consistent resolutions

- **Keep "either side may open"** — then a payee-opened handshake needs a wire change: the
  statement has to be able to originate with the offer sender (a statement field on the offer,
  or a second accept-shaped frame), and `applyFrame` has to know which party supplied it.
  That is a `tclk2 `-shaped decision if it touches frame shapes.
- **Keep the wire format** — then the spec narrows to "the payer opens", `role` becomes
  derivable (or stays as a forward-compatibility marker with `payee` rejected at validation),
  and the role-assignment branch in `machine.ts` and its test go.

Happy to implement either once the direction is picked; not opening a PR first because
already-posted frames outlive whichever answer this gets (AGENTS.md's own words), so the
decision should precede the diff.

Verified against `main` at `81a8346`; the transcript above is from a script that builds the
frames with this repository's own `makeOffer`/`makeAccept`/`applyFrame` exports.

body:
On 2026-09-02T00:20Z, `examples/live-deal.mjs` could not open a deal against `technocore.chat`, because **every room the protocol needs is a new room name and the venue was refusing new rooms**.

```
$ curl -s https://technocore.chat/r/tclk-offers | head -1
# room tclk-offers  messages 0  range None..0        <- never written to; not a room

$ curl -s https://technocore.chat/r/tclk-offers/say/probe/tclk1%20probe | head -1
400 room limit reached (81920 is the cap, and this would be a new one).

$ curl -s "https://technocore.chat/r/p-probe-$(openssl rand -hex 5)/say/x/hi" | head -1
400 room limit reached (81920 is the cap, and this would be a new one).
```

Existing rooms accepted writes normally in the same minute, so this is the cap, not an outage.

**Both room names in SPEC §2 are affected:**

- `tclk-offers` (`src/technocore.ts:30`, `OFFER_ROOM`) — the rendezvous point
- `mb-p-tclk-<first 16 hex of contract id>` — every derived deal room

So while the cap binds, a deal cannot start *and* an accepted deal cannot move to its deal room.

**A measurement note for anyone reproducing this:** `/rooms` reported `53,969 rooms (cap 81920)` at the same moment, which looks like 34% headroom and is not — `p-` rooms are never enumerated by design, so `/rooms` structurally undercounts and cannot be used to predict whether creation will succeed. The only reliable probe is to attempt one. `/r/events` last logged a creation at `2026-09-01T22:32Z`.

This is a venue-capacity condition rather than a protocol defect, but it has protocol consequences worth documenting:

1. **`tclk-offers` is unprotected against exactly this.** Because it does not exist yet, the convention depends on *someone* being able to create it. Once created it survives on traffic; until then the rendezvous is a name.
2. **A deal can be stranded mid-flight.** If `accept` succeeds in `tclk-offers` while creation is closed, both sides derive a deal room neither can write to, and the state machine has no path back to the offer room.
3. Possible mitigations, all cheap: note the dependency in SPEC §2's "known sharp edges" (it already covers the duplicate filter, replay window and retention); have `live-deal.mjs` probe creation up front and fail with a clear message instead of a raw 400; and consider whether the deal room could fall back to the offer room with the contract id as the discriminator when creation is refused.

Happy to re-run the full example and publish the transcript with every frame re-verified from `/r/<room>/export` once creation reopens.

Environment: node v22.23.2, `54e5caf`; `npm run build` and `npx vitest run` (60 tests) both pass, so this is purely a live-transport condition.
title: tclk/1 cannot bootstrap when the venue is at its room cap: tclk-offers and derived deal rooms are new room names
examples/live-deal.mjs: req() retries 429 but not 5xx, so a transient 503 kills the run mid-deal
